title: The Zoom Class
synopsis: There are two pandemics. They're happening in the same country, in the same cities, at the same time, and they're being experienced so differently ...
preview: There are two pandemics. They're happening in the same country, in the same cities, at the same time, and they're being experienced so differently ...
content:
There are two pandemics. They're happening in the same country, in the same cities, at the same time, and they're being experienced so differently that they might as well be occurring on separate planets.

In one pandemic, life continues. It continues from home, which is inconvenient and sometimes lonely, and the work gets done. The laptop opens in the morning. The meetings happen on screens. The salary arrives, the mortgage gets paid, the children attend school online, which is worse but manageable. The supermarket delivers. The pandemic is an interruption and a reconfiguration and, for some people, an improvement - no commute, more time at home, the flexibility that decades of requests to management never secured and a virus achieved in a fortnight.

In the other pandemic, you go to work or you don't eat. You stand at a register, drive a truck, stock a warehouse, clean a hospital, care for the elderly in facilities where this virus kills with particular efficiency. You can't work from home because your work is physical and located and embodied. Your job requires your body to be in a specific place, and that place is where other bodies are, and some of those bodies are infected.

The first group - the Zoom class, as I've started thinking of them - are largely insulated from the physical reality of the thing. They experience it as a disruption to convenience. The second group experience it as a disruption to their safety.

Our language obscures this rather neatly. We call them essential workers, which sounds like a compliment and functions as a designation. Essential means required. Required means you don't get to stay home. The word that sounds like respect is operating as an instruction.

I've been watching the divide from Adelaide, where lockdowns have been lighter than Melbourne's and the dynamics are identical. The people I know in knowledge work have adapted and some have thrived. The digital tools were already mature - the pandemic only removed the institutional resistance to using them. Productivity by most measures has held or improved. The Zoom class has discovered that the office was frequently unnecessary, that the commute was wasted time, and that the open-plan layout was a productivity disaster tolerated because it was cheaper than giving people doors.

The people I know in physical work haven't thrived. They've endured. The nurse taking extra shifts because colleagues are isolating. The delivery driver handling a hundred packages a day, each potentially contaminated. The retail worker enforcing mask mandates on hostile customers for seventeen dollars an hour. They're exhausted, underpaid relative to the risk they carry, and invisible to the Zoom class in the way infrastructure is always invisible to the people it holds up.

**Why This Doesn't Heal**

What I want to argue is that the division is permanent, because the temporary framing lets everyone believe that when the pandemic ends the divide closes. It won't. The pandemic didn't create this. It revealed and accelerated something already forming, and the acceleration is going to continue after the virus stops being interesting.

The Zoom class will absorb AI tools into their work over the next few years. They'll become more productive, their skills will compound, and they'll work from anywhere and live where they choose, participating in a global labour market where talent commands a premium and location stops mattering.

The physical workers face a different trajectory entirely. Automation will arrive - gradually and then suddenly - for exactly the tasks that currently require their presence. Autonomous vehicles displacing drivers. Automated warehouses displacing pickers. Robotic systems displacing manufacturing workers. And when that happens, the cognitive ladder previous generations climbed, from manual work to administrative work to professional work, won't be there, because these same AI systems will already be sitting on the lower rungs.

That's the part I find genuinely difficult. Every previous wave of displacement had somewhere for people to go, and the somewhere was up. This one removes the destination and the ladder at roughly the same time, and we're planning for it with retraining programs designed for a world where the retraining leads somewhere.

The social contract between the two groups is dissolving in the meantime. They inhabit the same country, pay into the same system and vote in the same elections, and their daily realities have diverged so completely that the shared experience underpinning social cohesion is disappearing. They don't understand each other's lives. They don't share each other's risks. They increasingly don't inhabit the same economy at all.

In Australia this maps onto geography, which makes it worse. The inner cities where knowledge workers cluster are becoming islands of affluence and connectivity. The suburbs and regions where physical work concentrates face stagnant wages, rising costs, declining services, and the slow erosion of the clubs and churches and pubs that once provided social infrastructure.

**The Thing Worth Fixing First**

Every society tells itself a story about shared fate. The Australian version - the fair go, the idea that work leads to a reasonable life whatever your starting point - has been under strain for decades, and the pandemic has shown how thin the remaining threads are. The Zoom class doesn't need the fair go to be true in order to believe in it. The essential class needs it to be true.

If I were choosing one place to push, it would be paying for risk properly. Not applause, not essential worker designations, not one-off bonuses. A statutory risk loading on work that cannot be done remotely during a declared emergency, paid automatically, calculated in advance, and legislated before the next crisis rather than negotiated during it.

I'd start there because it's the one intervention that operates in the actual currency of the divide. The Zoom class was compensated by the pandemic - lower costs, more time, better conditions. The essential class was taxed by it, in exposure and exhaustion, and we settled the account with words. A pre-legislated loading turns the designation into a payment, which is what it should have been from the first week. It doesn't fix automation, or geography, or the ladder. It fixes the specific injustice we can see clearly right now, while we can still see it.

The arrangement we have has a certain stability, so long as nobody looks at it too directly. The Zoom class makes policy. The essential class makes the policy possible. The pandemic forced everyone to look, briefly, and that attention is the perishable thing here - it will fade faster than the divide it exposed.

What we do with what we've seen decides whether the gap narrows or hardens into something permanent. I have my suspicions about which way it goes. I'd very much like to be wrong, and the useful thing about this particular problem is that being wrong is entirely within our power to arrange.
